concept_edges.logic: x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
Relational operators compare two numbers to give a boolean; logical operators combine booleans into one boolean.
A double holds a number with a fractional part; a boolean holds only true or false.
An int holds an integer and is a numeric type for computing with numbers; a boolean holds only true or false and is used for computing with logical values.
With two ints, a / b drops the fractional part; if either a or b is a double, a / b keeps the fractional part.
An operator combines operand values a and b into a new value, so operators build larger expressions from smaller ones.
For ints a and b, / gives the whole quotient q and % gives the remainder r, so that a = b * q + r.
new fills every slot with the type's default value: 0, 0.0, false or null.
{v0, v1, ..., vk} is a shorthand that creates an array of length k + 1 and fills it in one step.
An array must be created with new before any of its elements a[i] can be accessed.
double[] a; declares the array name and type; a = new double[N]; then creates the array.
i++ is shorthand for the assignment i = i + 1.
A comparison such as a < b takes two numbers and produces a boolean result.
&&, || and ! are the operations defined on the boolean type: they take booleans and give a boolean.
A while tests its boolean condition before every pass and stops the first time it evaluates to false.
A comparison such as x < y produces a boolean result; comparisons together with boolean logic provide the basis for decision-making.
A data structure organizes many values of a data type; the array holds a sequence of values of one type.
Java has eight primitive data types (boolean, char, byte, short, int, long, float, double); each, like any data type, is a set of values and a set of operations on those values.
A variable must be declared before an assignment can store a value into it.
Comparison operators build expressions whose value is a boolean, so one must already know what an expression is to understand a < b.
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) gives i every valid index exactly once, in increasing order.
A variable declared in the for header exists only from its declaration to the end of the for statement's block.
A declaration pairs a type with an identifier, e.g. int count;.
Every variable is named by an identifier that follows the naming rules.
A traversal uses the loop variable i as the index, so a[i] reaches a different element on each pass.
Normalising must divide as doubles, because with two ints counts / total truncates to 0 whenever counts < total.
A variable of type t is given a value of type t, often written as a literal.
&&, || and ! combine conditions p and q into one larger condition that is still true or false.
The for header is exactly the three control slots, and the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass.
The loop update i = i + 1 comes first; ++ (and +=) are then introduced as shorthand for that update.
The init, condition and update all act on the loop variable: the init sets it, the condition tests it, the update changes it.
boolean is one of the eight primitive types, the one used for true-false values.
double is one of the eight primitive types, the one used for real (floating-point) numbers.
int is one of the eight primitive types, the one used for integers.
A literal is the source-code form of a value of some type, and the way it is written fixes that type: 1234 is an int, 3.14 a double, true a boolean, 'c' a char.
A statement block is a sequence of statements, each terminated by a semicolon, enclosed in braces; the body of main() is such a sequence.
Control flow is the order in which statements run.
Each row of the transition matrix must be a probability distribution, so counts[i][j] is divided by outDegree[i] (scaled by .90, plus .10/N) to make row i sum to 1.
Assignment needs a declared variable on its left side to store the computed value into.
An expression can be a literal, a variable, or operations on them; we compute with a variable by using its name in an expression.
The loop body is the block of statements that a while (or for) loop repeats on each pass.
A loop variable is a counter that the loop initializes, tests in its condition and increments on each pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Declaring sum inside the loop body keeps a running total across passes.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The accumulator must be declared and initialised before the loop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A true/false question is answered with arithmetic (e.g. 1 for true).
misconceptions.correct_rule: A logic question is written as a boolean expression whose value is true or false.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: "10" - 1 or "6" * "2" works because the strings look like numbers.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Arithmetic operators other than + are not defined for Strings; a String of digits must first be converted to a number, e.g. with Integer.parseInt.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a(i) accesses element i of an array.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Array elements are accessed with square brackets, a[i].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Arrays are created without the new keyword.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An array is created with new (or with an initializer list in a declaration).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The number of brackets in an array type or initializer is the array's length.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Brackets give the number of dimensions; the length is set at creation.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Creating a big array with new takes no time because the elements are not set yet.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java initializes every element when the array is created, so creation takes time proportional to its length.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]].
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array can hold elements of any type.
misconceptions.correct_rule: All elements of an array have the declared element type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The first element of a is a[1].
misconceptions.correct_rule: Numbering begins with 0; the first element is a[0].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: initializer values go in [] instead of {}
misconceptions.correct_rule: Starting values go in braces, like int[] a = {v0, v1};.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array cannot have length 0.
misconceptions.correct_rule: new int[0] is a legal array of length 0.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an ArrayList is an array (borderline; beyond Chapter 1 CS1)
misconceptions.correct_rule: An array has a fixed length and uses [] and .length; an ArrayList can grow and uses get, set and size().

misconceptions.wrong_belief: new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The slots are 0 to n - 1.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Using an array means every cell must be scanned.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Arrays allow random access: a[i] reaches one element directly, and a loop visits only the elements the task needs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an array grows as you add elements
misconceptions.correct_rule: An array's length is fixed when it is created, so a[n] throws an exception.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: = compares two values instead of assigning
misconceptions.correct_rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Assigns a new value to a variable declared final.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A final variable cannot be reassigned after it is initialized; the compiler reports an error.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model).
misconceptions.correct_rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: assigning a reference copies the object
misconceptions.correct_rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: b = a exchanges the values of a and b.
misconceptions.correct_rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression
misconceptions.correct_rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a = b copies the value of a into b.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Changing the loop variable inside the body does not affect the loop condition; the loop still runs its planned number of times.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The condition is tested with the current value of the variable, including changes made in the body.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: true and false are the numbers 1 and 0, so a boolean can be used in arithmetic.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The boolean data type has only two possible values: true and false, and they are not numbers in Java.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a || b && c is evaluated left to right as (a || b) && c.
misconceptions.correct_rule: && binds tighter than ||, so it is a || (b && c).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Indenting several statements under an if or for makes them all part of its body, even without braces.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Without braces only the first statement belongs to the if/for; the rest run once, after it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a^2 computes a squared.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java has no exponent operator; ^ is exclusive or, and a * a or Math.pow(a, 2) computes a squared.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: (double) (3 / 5) is 0.6.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The integer division 3 / 5 = 0 happens before the cast, so the result is 0.0.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: 90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100.
misconceptions.correct_rule: a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped.
misconceptions.correct_rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you must write == true / == false to test a boolean
misconceptions.correct_rule: if (b) already tests b, so writing == true adds nothing.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The declaration only names the array; until new (or an initializer) creates it, using a[i] gives a 'variable might not have been initialized' compile-time error.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes name = value; to declare a new variable.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A declaration needs a type: type name = value;

misconceptions.wrong_belief: int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A declaration creates the variable (its storage) with its type; assignment later puts a value in it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Leaves a traversal loop with return before every element has been processed.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A result that depends on all elements is known only after the loop ends.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i.
misconceptions.correct_rule: a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is used.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: X[i] names the whole array, not one element.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The array is a; a[i] is the single element at index i.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes else (x > 0) with a condition but no if.
misconceptions.correct_rule: else takes no condition; use else if (x > 0).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: == compares contents (the String == bug)
misconceptions.correct_rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: .equals() compares references, not contents
misconceptions.correct_rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes a + b = c; or 7 = a; as if = were a math equation.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The left side of an assignment must be a single variable; only the right side can be an expression.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Math.sqrt(2) * Math.sqrt(2) == 2 is true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A double is an approximation, so the product is close to 2 but not equal to 2.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes for (int i = 0, i < n, i++).
misconceptions.correct_rule: The three parts of a for header are separated by semicolons; commas only separate several statements inside the init or the update part.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The body of a for statement executes at most once.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The body of a for statement runs once for every pass on which the condition is true, which can be many times.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: i declared in the for header can still be used after the loop has ended.
misconceptions.correct_rule: i declared in the for header exists only inside the loop, so using it after the loop does not compile.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Some loops can only be written with for, others only with while.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa; for just packages init, test and update.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever).
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An if inside a loop body runs its branch on every pass without testing its condition.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The if condition is tested again on every pass, with the current values, so the branch runs only on passes where it is true.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an if body repeats while its condition holds
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if body runs at most once; only a loop repeats its body.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Indents nested blocks inconsistently, so the visual nesting differs from the real nesting.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Indent consistently, one level deeper for each nested block, so the layout shows the real nesting; the compiler ignores indentation.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: i++ increases i by 2.
misconceptions.correct_rule: i++ (and ++i) increases i by exactly 1.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value.
misconceptions.correct_rule: i is a position; a[i] is the value stored at that position.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a condition that never goes false still terminates
misconceptions.correct_rule: A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An int result that is too large is automatically stored as a bigger number.
misconceptions.correct_rule: int arithmetic is 32-bit; a result outside the range wraps around.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: 10 / 3 evaluates to 3.333....
misconceptions.correct_rule: Dividing two ints gives an int: the fractional part is discarded.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: probabilities computed with integer division stay correct
misconceptions.correct_rule: counts[i][j] / outDegree[i] with two int operands is integer division and gives 0 whenever counts < outDegree; SW's Transition avoids it by multiplying by .90 first, and RandomSurfer casts with (double) freq[i] / T.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: If my loop never ends, the compiler or Java will warn me.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java cannot detect infinite loops in general; you must check that the loop condition eventually becomes false.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a large integer literal is automatically long
misconceptions.correct_rule: A sequence of digits is an int literal only if its value falls within the int range; for larger values the book advises the long type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Changing a later literal to 100.0 fixes an earlier int division.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The int division happens first; the double must be in the division itself.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: < and > mean the same thing (or a < b means a is greater than b).
misconceptions.correct_rule: a < b is true when a is smaller than b; a > b when a is larger.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: local variables get a default value on their own
misconceptions.correct_rule: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A while or for body runs zero times when the condition is false at the start.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations
misconceptions.correct_rule: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Some statements inside the braces of a loop body are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: If a loop condition is false at first but would become true later, the loop still runs (it repeats or skips until the condition is true, then runs until it is false).
misconceptions.correct_rule: A while loop whose condition is false at the first test runs zero times; nothing later revives it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: How many times a loop runs is decided by what the program is meant to do, so it may go on after its condition is false.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The loop runs only while its condition is true when tested; it stops at the first false test.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A test made once is an if; a loop repeats.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Initializes the flag before the loop so that the loop condition is already false, and the loop body never runs.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A while loop tests its condition before the first pass: if the values set before the loop make the condition false, the body never runs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A loop prints the same thing on every pass; the changing loop variable does not affect what the body does.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The body uses the current value of the loop variable, so its output can differ on each pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A loop runs its first body statement all N times, then its second body statement all N times.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each pass runs the whole body in order, so the body statements interleave: S1, S2, S1, S2, ...

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--).
misconceptions.correct_rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: For and while loops end when the condition becomes true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A for or while loop ends when its condition becomes false.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The update expression is the same on every pass; the loop variable changes by the rule written in the update.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The for variable i is a new variable on every pass rather than one variable changed by the update.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The for variable i is created once by the init, and the update changes that same variable on every pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The range of the loop variable limits the values that can be read or printed inside the loop.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The loop variable only counts passes; other values read or printed in the body are not bounded by it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A while loop ends by itself even if nothing in the body changes the variable tested in the condition.
misconceptions.correct_rule: If no statement in the body changes a variable in the condition, a condition that was true stays true and the loop never ends.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you need ? : to do the same
misconceptions.correct_rule: ok = (x > y); already gives the boolean, so the ? : is unnecessary.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you need an if to turn a boolean expression into a boolean
misconceptions.correct_rule: ok = (x > y); stores the result of the comparison directly.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Omits braces around a single-statement body of if, for or while.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Braces are optional for a single-statement body, but using them anyway avoids bugs when statements are added later.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes Sytem.out.prinln or a misspelled variable name.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Every name must be spelled exactly, including capitalization.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable can contain more than one value.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A variable holds exactly one value at a time; assigning a new value replaces the old one.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a 2-D array is one thing, not an array of arrays
misconceptions.correct_rule: A 2-D array is an array of m row arrays, so a[i] is a 1-D array of length n.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Naming a variable max (or average) makes it hold the largest value (or the average) without code that computes it.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A name only labels the variable for human readers; only the statements that assign to it decide its value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: new int[n] with a negative n creates an empty array.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Creating an array with a negative length throws NegativeArraySizeException at run time.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a % b is never negative, and integer division of a negative number rounds down.
misconceptions.correct_rule: a / b rounds toward 0 and a % b takes the sign of a: -14 / 3 is -4 and -14 % 3 is -2.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Several conditions combine into one boolean expression with && and ||, e.g. if (x == 0 && y == 0).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The slots of a new int[n] hold unpredictable values until assigned.
misconceptions.correct_rule: new fills every element with a default: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for String and other non-primitive types.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a single literal or variable "isn't an expression"
misconceptions.correct_rule: A single variable or literal is an expression whose value is just that value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Java has no float literals
misconceptions.correct_rule: A decimal literal ending in f is a float; without the f it is a double.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: multi-dimensional arrays must be rectangular
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each row a[i] is its own array, so rows can have different lengths a[i].length.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Java has no long literals
misconceptions.correct_rule: An integer literal ending in L is a long.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: keywords may be reused as identifiers
misconceptions.correct_rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them)
misconceptions.correct_rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: & is only a bitwise operator
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java also has a & operator, which the book does not use; logical and is written &&.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable
misconceptions.correct_rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first
misconceptions.correct_rule: In f(g(x)), g(x) is evaluated first and its result is passed to f.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: () are optional on a no-argument call like println
misconceptions.correct_rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: i = i++ increases i by 1.
misconceptions.correct_rule: i++ evaluates to the old value, so i = i++ stores the old value back.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: ++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass
misconceptions.correct_rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Both increment i, but ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs.
misconceptions.correct_rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes int x = 5; ... int x = 10; to change x.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A declaration gives a variable its name and type; a later change of value is an assignment statement such as x = 10;, not a second declaration.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: 9 % 5 means 9 minus 5 (a % b subtracts b from a).
misconceptions.correct_rule: % gives the remainder after integer division: 9 % 5 is 4 because 9 = 1 * 5 + 4, and 17 % 5 is 2, not 12.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Reading a second input value into a variable that already holds one is an error, so the program cannot run.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A later read simply overwrites the variable's current value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A return inside a loop does not end the loop; it sets a value each pass (the last one is returned) or returns several values.
misconceptions.correct_rule: When return executes, the method ends at once, so the loop stops on that pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes =< or => instead of <= and >=.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The operators are written <= and >=.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A page with no outgoing links can have an all-zero row.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each row is a probability distribution; a page with no links is made equally likely to move to every page.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: if (x > 0); System.out.println("positive"); prints only for positive x.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The ; ends the if with an empty statement, so the next line always runs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Puts a ; right after for (...) or while (...).
misconceptions.correct_rule: A ; right after the loop header is a null (empty) loop body, so the statements written after it are not repeated by the loop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: & and | are the same as && and || for conditions, so either can be used.
misconceptions.correct_rule: && and || skip the right operand when the left decides the result; & and | always evaluate both, which fails when the right side depends on the left (e.g. x != 0 & y / x > 1).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A task that must be repeated is written once, without a loop, as if one pass were enough.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A step that must happen several times (or an unknown number of times) needs a loop such as while or for; code without a loop runs once.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Values changed by one pass of a loop (other than the loop variable) do not affect later passes.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each pass starts from the state left by the previous pass, so a change in one pass carries into the next ones.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A statement placed after the if statement belongs to its branch, so it runs only when the condition is true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The branch ends at its closing brace (or after its single statement); the next statement runs whatever the condition was.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A statement written after the loop is repeated with the loop body.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The body ends at the closing brace (or after its single statement); code after it runs once, after the loop ends.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a statement runs without the ;
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement must end with ;, otherwise javac reports ';' expected.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Statements in a program can run in any order.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: String is a primitive type like int.

level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
wrong rule: a = b copies the value of a into b. Right rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.
wrong rule: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model). Right rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.
wrong rule: b = a exchanges the values of a and b. Right rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
wrong rule: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved. Right rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.

Points to LT (evaluate the right side with current values, then overwrite the left variable). Applied unevenly, a student traces one segment correctly but reads the next as simultaneous equations or as a swap, giving 15 and 15 for one segment and 5 and 10 for the other. (here mixing in: "= stores the expression itself, not its computed value")
wrong rule: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values. Right rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.
wrong rule: assigning a reference copies the object. Right rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

Swapping the two sides (a = b versus b = a) changes which variable changes. Reordering assignments changes the final values. An assignment cannot be undone, because the old value is lost unless it was first saved in a temporary.
wrong rule: a = a + b adds the arrays element by element. Right rule: Java has no arithmetic on whole arrays; write a loop that adds a[i] + b[i] for each i.

wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.
wrong rule: Using an array means every cell must be scanned. Right rule: A traversal may cover only part of the array or stop early (as in a search); indexing reaches single elements directly.

Points to LT: initialize i, test, run the body with the current i, update, test again. Inconsistent application: on some passes the update is applied before the body, or a[i] is traced with the previous i. (here mixing in: "a = a + b adds the arrays element by element")
wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n.
wrong rule: After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i. Right rule: a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is used.

Conservation: running the index downward (a.length-1 to 0) visits the same set of elements in reverse order, harmless for a sum but not for a shift. Starting at 1 or stopping at a.length-1 drops an element. Invariant: before pass i, elements 0..i-1 have been processed.
wrong rule: a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference. Right rule: A reference variable holds only a reference to the object, which is stored separately.
wrong rule: A variable can contain more than one value. Right rule: A variable holds exactly one value at a time; assigning a new value replaces the old one.

wrong rule: The computer recognises that one variable plays two roles, e.g. input value and running total, and keeps the values apart; it knows which variable is the counter and which the sum. Right rule: A variable holds one value at a time; each role (input, counter, running total) needs its own variable and explicit update.
wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

wrong rule: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global. Right rule: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

wrong rule: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations. Right rule: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value.

wrong rule: Naming a variable max (or average) makes it hold the largest value (or the average) without code that computes it. Right rule: A name only labels the variable for human readers; only the statements that assign to it decide its value.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.

wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.
wrong rule: local variables get a default value on their own. Right rule: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.
wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

wrong rule: int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned. Right rule: A declaration creates the variable (its storage) with its type; assignment later puts a value in it.
wrong rule: Reading a second input value into a variable that already holds one is an error, so the program cannot run. Right rule: A later read simply overwrites the variable's current value.

wrong rule: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]]. Right rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.

Renaming a variable consistently keeps behavior. Reordering statements that write and read it changes results (a = b; b = a; is not a swap). Moving its declaration into a loop body narrows its scope and resets it on every pass.
